title: Trace-the-Data Investigation (Lab)
summary: Students run three controlled single data swaps on the ripeness sorter, log the before-and-after outcomes, and use that evidence to identify and verify the most influential change.
objectives: Change the data in a worked solution and observe and record the effect on the outcome.
Identify which single data change most alters the outcome, and explain why.

body: In the Core lesson you predicted how a data change would move the outcome. A prediction is only a guess until you test it. Today you run a fair test: change one thing, watch the outcome, and let the evidence tell you which data matters most.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can run a controlled data change and record the outcome before and after.
I can compare data changes and identify which one moved the outcome the most.
I can explain, using my recorded evidence, why that change had the biggest effect.

terms.definition: Changing one thing at a time so you know what caused the result.
The outcome measured just before and just after a single change.
How far the outcome moved because of a change.
Having a large effect on the outcome.
To re-test and confirm an effect is real, not a one-off.

sections.heading: Change one thing at a time
body: To find out how much a data batch matters, you must isolate it. Measure the outcome **before**, change only that one batch, and measure again. The difference is the influence of that batch.
If you change two batches at once and the outcome moves, you cannot tell which batch did it. A fair test changes one variable at a time - the same rule scientists use in any experiment.

sections.heading: Evidence beats opinion
body: Your log is your evidence. Without a written before-and-after, you are relying on memory, and memory blurs across many swaps.

Once you have run several swaps, the most [[influential]] batch is the one with the biggest [[shift]]. [[Verify]] it by re-running on a fresh fruit - if the effect repeats, you have proof, not a coincidence.

sections.label: Hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Work in threes with roles: swapper, recorder, checker. You will run three single data swaps, log each outcome, and find the most influential change.
items: Write your Core prediction at the top of the log.
Record the BEFORE outcome for your test fruit.
Swap in one data batch and record the AFTER outcome.
Note the shift: none, a little, or a lot.
Repeat for two more single swaps.
Rank the swaps and star the most influential.
Verify the winner on a fresh fruit and write your conclusion.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Did the evidence match your prediction? Where did it surprise you?
Why might a small batch beat a large one for influence?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write your evidence-based conclusion about the most influential data change.
Note one thing a fair test taught you that a guess could not.

questions.prompt: Run three single swaps: for each swap, record the before outcome, the after outcome, and the size of the shift. Change only one batch at a time.
questions.lookFor: One batch changed at a time with a clean before value recorded before the swap, not filled in afterwards. Changing several batches at once means the outcome cannot be attributed and the swap should be redone.

questions.prompt: Name and verify the winner: state which swap was most influential, justify it from your log, and describe how you verified it on a fresh fruit.
questions.stem:
The most influential swap was ___
My log shows ___
I verified it by ___
questions.lookFor: The winner is the batch that filled the biggest data gap - typically the green-date batch - justified from the logged before/after shifts rather than opinion, and confirmed by a re-test on a fresh fruit that shows the effect repeats.

questions.prompt: Investigation log: log every single swap and its effect so you can rank them fairly. Use the columns Swap (one batch) | Before outcome | After outcome | Shift size | Rank.
questions.lookFor: Every row records one batch only, with both before and after outcomes filled in and a shift size (none / a little / a lot). A missing before value or a muddled swap makes the ranking unreliable.

questions.prompt: Exit ticket: state the most influential data change you found and give the recorded evidence that proves it.
questions.lookFor: Evidence, not opinion: the named swap is backed by the before/after shift written in the log, and ideally by the repeat result from the verification run.

questions.prompt: Challenge (stretch): design a data swap you predict will produce zero outcome change, then test it. Explain why some data has no influence on this solution.
questions.lookFor: A swap that only adds more of what the sorter already has plenty of - for example another brown-date batch - with the explanation that it repeats a pattern the model already learned, so it fills no gap and moves nothing.
